summary: This note describes a comfrey trial run by the author, inspired by Lawrence D Hills, to measure biomass yield, fertility benefits for crops, attractiveness to wildlife, and effects on soil. It records 2016 and 2017 harvest weights from the 'Bocking 14' comfrey bed, which was fed lawn clippings and cut four or five times per season. It also tracks soil pH and nutrient results from samples sent to NAAS for analysis between 2015 and 2018.
one_line: A two-year comfrey trial recording biomass cuts, lawn-clipping inputs, wildlife observations and soil pH results from 2015 to 2018.
key_facts: The comfrey trials were inspired by the work of Lawrence D Hills (1911–1991), who researched comfrey extensively.
The trials aimed to measure how much biomass comfrey produces, how well it fertilises crops, how attractive it is to garden wildlife, and whether it benefits soils.
The 2016 'Bocking 14' comfrey bed produced a total of 96.92 kg over four cuts, or 2.31 kg per plant.
In 2016 the highest single cut was 32.2 kg on 06.06.16, with 0.77 kg per plant.
The 2017 'Bocking 14' bed produced a total of 99.28 kg over five cuts, or 2.2 kg per plant.
The bed was cut four or five times per season, and lawn trimmings were applied to the surface after each cut.
Lawn clippings totalled 480 L in 2016 and 570 L in 2017.
In 2017 the bed produced enough mulch to cover 18.5 m2 with a 10-15 cm deep layer of leaves.
The Hills bed measured 13 m2, was 10 m x 1.3 m, held 42 plants, and had a planting distance of 60-70 cm.
Casual observations recorded many spiders in the undergrowth, ladybirds, and many species of bees on the comfrey plants.
Native plants growing among the comfrey included Arctium lappa, Cichorium intybus and Sonchus spp. in 2016, and Daucus carota, Mentha longifolia and Prunus institia were added in 2017.
Soil pH (KCl) was 5.69 in March 2015 before planting and 6.67 in November 2016 after the first season of cuts.
Soil pH (KCl) was 5.85 in March 2017 and 6.54 in March 2018.
Soil samples were sent for analysis to NAAS of the Ministry of Agriculture and Food.
The site is recorded at latitude 41, elevation 580, average annual rainfall 588, in a market garden location at Shipka.
